\]

Then \(1/2<s\le1\), and the elementary pointwise inequality
\((1+|x|)^s\le(1+|x|)^{s_0}\) gives \(u_0\in L_s^2\).  This monotonicity
bridge, including measurability of the reweighted representative, is proved
internally before it is used.  All proof sections below use \(s\) as the
working Wu exponent; \(s_0\) remains the exponent in the theorem's target
hypothesis.  Since \((1+|x|)^{s_0}\ge1\), (0.3) also implies
\(u_0\in L^2\), as required by Chen's flow theorem.

For later reference, here is the complete internal weight bridge.  Put
\(w(x)=1+|x|\).  If \(r\le q\) and \(w^qf\in L^2\), then

\[
 w^rf=w^{r-q}(w^qf),\qquad
 |w^rf|\le |w^qf|,
 \tag{0.3c}
\]

because \(w\ge1\) and \(w^{r-q}\le1\).  The first identity also proves
strong measurability: \(w^{r-q}\) is continuous and \(w^qf\) has a strongly
measurable representative.  Therefore \(L_q^2\subseteq L_r^2\).  Taking
\(r=0\) proves \(L_{s_0}^2\subseteq L^2\), and taking
\(r=\min\{s_0,1\}\) proves the reduction used above.  No external weighted
embedding theorem is used.

mathematical_input: Let s be a nonnegative real number and f:R -> R. Put w(x)=1+|x|. Suppose w(x)^s f(x) belongs to L2 for Lebesgue measure. Then f belongs to L2. Weighted L2 is interpreted using the given real representative and includes a.e. strong measurability of the weighted function.

source_steps.text: The weight w is positive and continuous. Its real power w^s is positive, so the inverse power is continuous. Multiplying the measurable weighted representative by this inverse gives f and proves a.e. strong measurability of f.
Since w>=1 and s>=0, w^s>=1. Hence |f(x)|<=|w(x)^s f(x)| at every x.
Apply L2 domination using this bound and the measurability just proved. This obtains unweighted L2 membership without adding it as an assumption.
